column1: # Shared aontu unit tests: the number model. Columns (tab-separated): name<TAB>mode<TAB>src<TAB>expect

# mode: canon = unify(src).canon == expect ; gen = generate(src) deep-equals JSON(expect) ; gens = generate(src) as compact JSON == expect byte for byte ; err = generate(src) errors, message contains expect
# See docs/design/number-model.md for the rules these rows pin.
# R1: a numeric literal has integer kind iff its source has no '.', its
# value is integral, and it lies within the int64 range. Otherwise it is
# number kind. (aontu has no negative literals -- '-' is an operator --
# so the int64 minimum is not expressible as an integer-kind literal.)
# R1 now runs BEHIND D7 (docs/design/number-tower.md): a literal whose
# value binary64 cannot hold exactly never becomes a value at all, so it
# never reaches the kind question. The rows below therefore all use
# literals that ARE exact -- 1e21 and 10^20 are exact and merely outside
# the int64 window, which is precisely what makes them number kind.
# `gens`, not `gen`, and the mode is the point: 2^53 is the first
# integer-kind value TypeScript generates as a `bigint` rather than a
# `number` (see IntegerVal.gen), and `gen` decodes its expectation with
# JSON.parse -- which yields a float64, so a bigint could never
# deep-equal it whatever the digits say. The assertion this row exists
# to make is unchanged: `& integer` still errors unless 2^53 has integer
# kind, which is R1's claim here. Only the comparison had to move to the
# bytes, for the same reason `gens` exists at all.
# FLIPPED by D7. 0x7fffffffffffffff is 2^63-1, which rounds UP to 2^63,
# so it is refused at parse and the conjunction never gets as far as the
# kind check this row used to pin ("Cannot unify scalar values", the R1
# out-of-int64 failure). What it pins now is the ORDER: the lossy-literal
# refusal fires ahead of unification. Its exact neighbour 2^63 is still
# a value and still fails the kind check -- hex-pow63-integer-err below.
# FLIPPED by D7. This row pinned the silent rounding that D7 abolishes:
# DIFFERENT number. It is refused now, and the hint names the escape.
# R2: negative zero never survives into the AST, generated output, or canon.
# R3: concrete scalars are identical only when kind and value both match,
# so an integer and a float disjunct member are distinct alternatives.
# R4: canon round-trips kind -- a number-kind value always renders with a
# fraction or an exponent, so parse(canon(v)) preserves the kind of v.
# R5: kind contagion -- no operator or function introduces a narrower kind
# than its operands. integer+integer is integer; any number operand makes
# the result a number; upper()/lower() preserve the argument's kind.
# R6: super(x) is the lattice-superior of its argument -- the kind of a
# concrete scalar. (1 is an integer literal, so super(1) is integer.)
# NaN and Infinity are NOT numeric literals in aontu: they carry no
# special lexing, so they are bare text and unify as strings. (There
# is no way to write a non-finite number: an overflowing literal is a
# Leading zeros are decimal, never octal (08 and 09 are 8 and 9, not
# errors). A LEADING dot is not a numeric literal at all -- a bare
# dotted word is a relative path reference, so .5 is an unresolvable
# A numeric map KEY is not a number: the key keeps its source text
# verbatim, so it is never normalised through the number model.
# There are no negative literals: `-` is a prefix operator. It binds
# TIGHTER than `+`, `&` and `|` (and looser than `.`), so `-1 & -1` is
# `(-1) & (-1)`, not `-(1 & -1)`. Negation never narrows the kind.
# Base prefixes (hex/octal/binary) are LOWER CASE ONLY: an upper-case
# prefix is not a number at all, it is text. That follows the canonical
# TypeScript lexer, whose number matcher spells the prefixes in lower
# case; the Go engine declines the same sources (numberExcluded in
# go/lang.go) so the two agree. Note it is the prefix LETTER only -- an
# upper-case exponent marker is accepted by both (exp-upper-canon).
# A based literal has no '.', so R1(b)+(c) alone decide its kind, once
# D7 has let it be a value at all: 0x8000000000000000 is 2^63, a power
# of two and therefore exact, and it is number kind because 2^63 is one
# past int64's maximum -- which is why it cannot unify with `integer`.
# FLIPPED by D7. This row canoned 0x7fffffffffffffff as the rounded
# There is no canon of a refused literal to pin instead, so the row
# becomes the err that pins the OTHER assertion D7 rows carry: the hint
# names `0d` as the way to write the exact integer.
# FLIPPED by @tabnas/parser 0.8.3. These rows used to assert that an
# UPPER-CASE base prefix lexes as TEXT -- `x:0X1F` was the string
# "0X1F" -- because the canonical TypeScript number matcher spelled the
# prefixes lower-case only, and go/lang.go mirrored the quirk with an
# upperBasePrefix exclusion so the ports would agree.
# That function documented its own exit condition: if the upstream TS
# lexer ever gained the upper-case spellings, delete it and let BOTH
# engines accept them, and these rows would fail loudly and say so.
# parser 0.8.3 gained them, these rows duly failed, and the exclusion is
# gone. `0X1F` is now 31 in both ports, as JavaScript itself always read
# it. The prefix LETTER was the only thing at issue -- an upper-case
# EXPONENT marker (1E21) was always accepted and is pinned by
# Now a NUMBER, so it meets the same two rules its lower-case twin does:
# D7 refuses a literal binary64 cannot carry exactly, and a number does
# not unify with `string`. Both rows previously passed only because the
# Digit separators are legal only as a SINGLE separator BETWEEN
# digits. A run that breaks the rule is not a number at all: the whole
# run falls through to text, so a typo surfaces as a string rather
# than silently becoming a different number (1__0 is "1__0", not 10).
# The base-prefixed edge cases are pinned at both magnitudes because
# a literal beyond int64 takes a separate lexer path in the Go port.
# FLIPPED by D7: 0xff_ffffffffffffff is 2^64-1 with a separator in it,
# and 2^64-1 is not exactly representable, so it is refused rather than
# rounded (scalar.tsv:hex-big-err is the same value without the
# separator). The row still does the job this block wants: an err naming
# the lossy-literal rule proves the separator run was LEXED AS A NUMBER,
# because a broken separator run falls through to text instead (compare
# sep-prefix-edge-big-text below, which is the string). The accepted big
# separator is pinned positively by the exact literal beside it.
# Exponent forms. The exponent marker may be upper or lower case and
# its sign is optional; an exponent alone never makes a literal number
# kind (R1 looks for a '.', not an 'e'), so 1e3 and even the
# UNDERFLOWING 1e-400 -- which is exactly 0 -- are integer kind and
# canon them without a ".0". An OVERFLOWING literal is a not_number
# A numeric builtin called with no argument is an invalid-arg error
# value, not an internal error: reading the argument off nothing used
# to throw in TypeScript, which the unifier could only report as an
# opaque internal failure while Go reported it cleanly.
